en: Puggalapaññatti Niddesa 3. The Exposition of the Designation of Persons by Threes (Tikapuggalapaññatti)
And what kind of person is one who has lost hope?

Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions; though not a recluse, he claims to be a recluse, and though not living the holy life, he claims to live the holy life; he is inwardly rotten, leaking, and filled with filth.
He hears:

“Such-and-such a monk, it is said, by the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwells therein.
It does not occur to him:

“When indeed shall I too, by the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, dwell therein?”
This person is called "hopeless.
And what kind of person is hopeful?
Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good character.
Then he hears:

"It is said that a certain monk, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, enters and dwells therein.
It occurs to him:

“Someday, indeed, may I too—through the destruction of the taints—realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, may I dwell therein.
This person is called one who has expectations.
And what kind of person is one whose expectations have vanished?

Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge.
He hears:

"It is said that a monk named so-and-so, through the destruction of the taints, has entered and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge."
It does not occur to him:

"When indeed shall I, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwell therein?
For what reason?
For whatever hope he previously had for liberation while not yet liberated has subsided.
This person is called "one whose hope has vanished.
In this regard, who are the three persons comparable to the sick?
There are three kinds of sick persons:
here, a certain sick person, whether obtaining suitable food or not obtaining suitable food,
whether obtaining suitable medicine or not obtaining suitable medicine, or whether obtaining a suitable attendant...
Or, failing to obtain a suitable attendant, he does not recover from that illness.
However, in this case, a certain sick person— whether obtaining or not obtaining suitable food,
whether obtaining or not obtaining suitable medicine, and whether obtaining or not obtaining a suitable [attendant]— does not recover from that illness.
Or, failing to obtain a suitable attendant, he recovers from that illness.

Furthermore, in this case, a certain sick person recovers from that illness even while obtaining suitable food but not obtaining it, or while obtaining suitable medicine but not obtaining it, or while obtaining a suitable attendant but not obtaining one.
In that regard, as for the sick person who recovers while obtaining suitable food but not obtaining it... [and so on].
If one does not obtain medicines, or does not obtain a suitable attendant, yet recovers from that illness— for this reason,
the Blessed One has authorized sick food, authorized medicine for the sick,
and authorized an attendant for the sick.
Furthermore, because of this sick person, other sick people should also be attended to.
In this very way, there are three types of persons comparable to the sick who exist and are found in the world.
Which three?
In this case, a certain person— whether obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata,
whether obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata—
does not enter into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
Furthermore, here a certain person— whether obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata or not obtaining a vision of the Tathāgata,
whether obtaining a hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining a hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata—
enters upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.

Now, here a certain person, whether obtaining the sight of the Tathāgata or not obtaining it, and whether obtaining the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining it, enters upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
In this regard, as for that person who, whether obtaining the sight of the Tathāgata or not obtaining it,
and whether obtaining the hearing of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining it, enters upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states:
It is with reference to this person that the Blessed One has authorized the teaching of the Dhamma; and with reference to this person, the Dhamma should also be taught to others.
These are the three types of persons comparable to the sick who exist and are found in the world.
And what is the person who is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī)?

Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body; and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed—this person is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
And what kind of person is one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto)?
In this case, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering";
and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen by him through wisdom.
They have become practiced; and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely exhausted—this person is called one who has attained through vision.
And what is the person liberated by faith?
Here, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ...

[and so on] ... and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and pursued by his wisdom; having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are utterly destroyed, yet he has not attained through vision—this person is called one "liberated by faith."
And what kind of person is one who speaks like excrement?

Here, a certain person is a liar; when summoned as a witness and questioned in an assembly, in a gathering, in the midst of kinsmen, in the midst of a company, or in the presence of the royal court, he is told:
"Come now, sir, speak whatever you know."
Thus, not knowing, he says, “I know”;
or knowing, he says, “I do not know”;
or not seeing, he says, “I see.”
Or, seeing, he says, "I do not see. Thus,
whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he speaks a deliberate lie—
he is called a person who "speaks dung."
And what kind of person is one who speaks like a flower?

Here, a certain person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech. Whether in an assembly, in a council, in the midst of kinsmen, in the midst of a guild, or in the royal court, when summoned and questioned as a witness—"Come now, good man, speak what you know"—he does not speak falsely.
Thus, not knowing, he says, "I do not know";
or, knowing, he says, "I know";
or, not seeing, he says, "I do not see."
Or, seeing, he says, "I see. Thus,
whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he does not speak a deliberate lie—
this person is called a "flower-speaker."
And what kind of person is one who speaks like honey?
Here, a certain person speaks such speech as is gentle, pleasant to the ear, endearing, heart-stirring, urbane, agreeable to many, and pleasing to many—
such a person is called "one who speaks like honey."
And what kind of person is one whose mind is like a festering sore?

Here, a certain person is prone to anger and full of resentment; even when spoken to only slightly, he becomes agitated, becomes angry, becomes malevolent, becomes stubborn, and manifests anger, hatred, and ill-will.
Just as a malignant sore, when touched with a stick or a pebble, discharges more pus; so too is such a person.

In the same way, here a certain person is prone to anger and full of resentment; even when spoken to slightly, he becomes agitated, angry, malicious, and stubborn, manifesting anger, hatred, and ill-will.
This person is said to be "one whose mind is like a sore.
And what is the person whose mind is like lightning?
Here, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
Just as a man with good eyesight might see forms through a gap in the darkness of the night by means of a flash of lightning, even so, here a certain person understands as it really is:
"This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—this person is called one whose mind is like lightning.
And what kind of person is one whose mind is like a thunderbolt?
Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
having entered upon them. Just as there is nothing that a diamond cannot shatter,

whether it be a gem or a stone, even so, here a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon them.
This person is called one whose mind is like a diamond.
And what kind of person is blind?
Here, a certain person does not possess such an eye as that by which one might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired.

Furthermore, he does not possess such an eye by which he might know wholesome and unwholesome states, know blameworthy and blameless states, know inferior and superior states, and know dark and bright states with their counterparts—
this person is called "blind. And what kind of person is "one-eyed"?
In this case, a certain person possesses such an eye by which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired;
yet he does not possess such an eye by which he would know wholesome and unwholesome states, know blameworthy and blameless states, know inferior and superior states,
or know dark and bright states with their counterparts— this person is called "one-eyed."
And what kind of person has two eyes?
Here, a certain person possesses such an eye by means of which he might acquire wealth not yet acquired, or increase wealth already acquired;

and he also possesses such an eye by means of which he would know wholesome and unwholesome states, know blameworthy and blameless states, know inferior and superior states, and know dark and bright states with their counterparts.
This person is called "one with two eyes.
And what kind of person has "downward-turned wisdom"?
Here, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The monks teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Yet, while sitting on that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he still does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Just as if a jar were turned upside down and the water poured into it would flow out and not remain there,
even so, here a certain person goes to the monastery frequently to hear the Dhamma from the presence of the bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end— with the right meaning and phrasing, and they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure.
While sitting on that seat, he does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he still does not attend to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
Such a person is called one "of inverted wisdom."
And what kind of person is one of "lapped wisdom"?
Here, a certain person goes frequently to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Seated on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
But having risen from that seat, he no longer attends to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to its middle, nor does he attend to its end.
It is just as if various kinds of snacks were piled up in a man's lap.
There are sesame seeds, rice grains, sweetmeats, and jujube fruits.
As he rises from that seat, he might scatter them through a lapse of mindfulness;
even so, a certain person here goes frequently to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The monks teach him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Seated on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to the middle, and he attends to the end.
But having risen from that seat, he no longer attends to the beginning of that discourse, nor does he attend to the middle, nor does he attend to the end.
This person is called one of "bowl-deep wisdom.
And what is the person of "vast wisdom"?
Here, a certain person goes to the monastery frequently to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

The monks teach him the Dhamma—beautiful in its beginning, beautiful in its middle, and beautiful in its conclusion—with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Seated on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
Just as water poured into an upright jar remains there and does not spill out, even so,
a certain person here goes to the monastery frequently to hear the Dhamma from the presence of the bhikkhus.

The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end— with the right meaning and phrasing, and they reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
Sitting on that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning of that discourse, he attends to its middle, and he attends to its end.
Such a person is called one of "broad wisdom."
And what kind of person is one who is not free from lust for sense pleasures and for existence?
Stream-enterers and once-returners—
these are called persons who are "not free from lust for sense pleasures and for existence."
And what kind of person is one who is free from lust for sensual pleasures but not free from lust for existence?
The non-returner—
this is called the person who is "free from lust for sensual pleasures but not free from lust for existence."
And what kind of person is one who is free from lust for sense pleasures and for existence?
The Arahant—
this is called the person who is "free from lust for sense pleasures and for existence."
And what kind of person is like a carving on stone?
Here, a certain person becomes angry frequently,
and that anger of his persists for a long time, throughout a long period.
Just as a scratch on a stone does not quickly disappear through wind or water, but remains for a long time,
even so, here a certain person is frequently angry,
and that anger of his persists for a long time.
This person is called one who is like a line on stone.
And what kind of person is like a line on earth?
Here, a certain person becomes angry frequently.
And his anger does not persist for long or remain for a great length of time.
Just as a line drawn on the earth is quickly destroyed by wind or water and does not endure for long,
even so, a certain person here frequently becomes angry.
And his anger does not persist for long or remain for a long time—
this person is called "one who is like a scratch on the earth.
And what kind of person is one who is like a scratch in water?
Here, a certain person, even when spoken to harshly, spoken to roughly, or spoken to unpleasantly, still blends, unites, and rejoices.
Just as a line drawn on water quickly dissolves and does not remain for long,
even so, a certain person here, even when spoken to harshly, spoken to roughly, or spoken to unpleasantly, still blends, unites, and rejoices.
This person is called “one who is like a drawing on water.
In this regard, what are the three persons who are like a cloth?
There are three kinds of cloths:
A new cloth is both ill-colored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value;
a middle-aged cloth is also ill-colored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value;
and even an old cloth is ill-colored, unpleasant to the touch, and of little value.
They either use an old book for wiping a cooking pot or they throw it away on a rubbish heap.
In the same way, there are these three types of persons resembling books found existing among the bhikkhus.
Which three?
Even if a bhikkhu is newly ordained, immoral, and of evil character, it is because of his ugliness.
Just as that cloth is ugly, so too is this person comparable to it.
And those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example—that leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
This is because of his painful nature to touch.
Just as that cloth is painful to touch, so too is this person.
And for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift yields neither great fruit nor great benefit for them.
This is because of his low worth.
Just as that cloth is of little value, so too is this person.
Even if he is a middle-ranking bhikkhu... [and so on].
Even if a monk is an elder, if he is immoral and of evil character, this is his ugliness.
Just as that cloth is ugly, so too is this person comparable to it.
And those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example—for them, that leads to harm and suffering for a long time.
This is because of his painful touch.
Just as that cloth is unpleasant to the touch, so too is this person.
Furthermore, for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift yields neither great fruit nor great benefit.
This is due to his worthlessness.
Just as that cloth is worthless, so too is this person comparable to it.
If such an elder bhikkhu speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha...
The monks said to him:
"What is the use of what you, a fool and an incompetent person, have to say? Do you really think that you too should speak?
Being angry and displeased, he utters such speech as would cause the Saṅgha to suspend him, like a rag upon a heap of refuse.
These three types of persons similar to cloth are found existing among the bhikkhus.
In this regard, what are the three types of persons similar to Kāsī cloth?
There are three kinds of Kāsī cloth:
Even new Kāsi cloth is both beautiful in color and pleasant to the touch, and it is of great value;

even middling Kāsi cloth is both beautiful in color and pleasant to the touch, and it is of great value; even worn-out Kāsi cloth is both beautiful in color and pleasant to the touch, and it is of great value.
Even worn-out cloth from Kāsi they wrap in precious jewels or place it in a perfumed casket.
In the same way, there are these three types of persons resembling cloth from Kāsi existing among the bhikkhus.
Which three?
Even if a bhikkhu is newly ordained, he is virtuous and of lovely character; this is his "golden quality.
Just as that cloth from Kāsī is beautiful in color, so too is this person.
And for those who serve him, associate with him, attend upon him, and follow his example, it leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
This is due to his pleasant touch.
Just as that Kāsī cloth has a pleasant touch, even so is this person.
And for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift becomes of great fruit and great benefit to them.
This is due to his great worth.
Just as that cloth from Kāsi is of great value, so too is this person.
And if a bhikkhu is of middling [worth]... [and so on].
If a monk is an elder who is virtuous and of good character, this constitutes his golden quality.
Just as that cloth from Kāsi is beautiful in color, so too is this person.
And for those who associate with him, frequent him, attend upon him, and follow his example, it leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
This is due to his pleasant touch.
Just as that Kāsī cloth is pleasant to the touch, even so is this person.
And for those from whom he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that gift becomes of great fruit and great benefit to them.
This is due to his great worth.
Just as that Kāsī cloth is of great value, so too is this person.
If such an elder bhikkhu speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the bhikkhus say this to him:
“Venerable sirs, be quiet; the elder bhikkhu is reciting the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
His words are accepted like Kāsī cloth placed in a perfumed casket.
These are the three types of persons resembling Kāsī cloth who exist among the bhikkhus.

And what kind of person is easy to measure? Here, a certain person is restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose of speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with faculties that are unrestrained—
this is called a person who is "easy to measure."
And what kind of person is difficult to measure?

Here, a certain person is not agitated, not haughty, not fickle, not talkative, and does not speak in a scattered manner; he is established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and has restrained sense faculties—this is called a person who is "difficult to measure."
And what kind of person is immeasurable?

Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it;
such a person is called "immeasurable."
And what kind of person is one who should not be associated with, should not be cultivated, and should not be honored?
Here, a certain person is inferior in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Such a person should not be associated with, should not be cultivated, and should not be honored, except out of compassion and out of sympathy.
And what kind of person is one who should be served, associated with, and attended upon?
Here, a certain person is equal in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Such a person is one who should be served, associated with, and attended upon.
For what reason?
"When we have attained equality in virtue, there will be talk of virtue among us, and that will be comfortable for us, and it will continue;
when we have attained equality in concentration, there will be talk of concentration among us, and that will be comfortable for us, and it will continue."
“Among those who have attained the commonality of wisdom, there will be discourse on wisdom for us; that will be comfortable for us, and it will continue for us.
Therefore, such a person should be served, befriended, and attended upon.
And what kind of person is one who, having honored and revered them, should be served, befriended, and attended upon?
In this case, a certain person is preeminent in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Such a person should be honored, revered, served, associated with, and attended upon. Why is that?
“Either I shall fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled here and there with wisdom;
either I shall fulfill the aggregate of concentration that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the aggregate of concentration that is already fulfilled here and there with wisdom;
either I shall fulfill the aggregate of wisdom that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support the aggregate of wisdom that is already fulfilled here and there with wisdom.”
Therefore, such a person should be honored, revered, served, associated with, and attended upon.
And what kind of person is to be loathed, not to be served, not to be associated with, and not to be attended upon?

Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspect conduct, secretive in his actions; one who is not a recluse but claims to be a recluse, who does not lead the holy life but claims to lead the holy life—one who is inwardly rotten, leaking, and filled with filth.
Such a person is to be loathed; he is not to be associated with, not to be frequented, and not to be honored.
Why is that? Because even if one does not follow the example of such a person’s views, nevertheless, an evil reputation spreads concerning him.
“A person with evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
Just as a snake that has entered a dung heap does not bite but nevertheless defiles it, even so,
although one may not follow the views of such a person, nevertheless an evil reputation spreads concerning them.
“A person who has evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
Therefore, such a person should be loathed; they should not be served, associated with, or attended upon.
And what kind of person should be looked upon with equanimity, and not served, associated with, or attended upon?

Here, a certain person is prone to anger and full of resentment; even when spoken to only slightly, he becomes agitated, becomes angry, becomes malevolent, becomes stubborn, and manifests anger, hatred, and ill-will.

Just as a festering sore, when touched with a stick or a pebble, discharges even more pus, even so does a certain person here who is prone to anger and full of resentment, even when spoken to only slightly.
He becomes resentful, agitated, malicious, and stubborn; he manifests anger, hatred, and resentment.
Just as a firebrand of *tinduka* wood, when struck with a stick or a potsherd, crackles and sizzles even more intensely, so too, a certain person here is prone to anger and full of distress;
even when addressed with only a little, he becomes resentful, agitated, malicious, and stubborn, manifesting anger, hatred, and resentment.
Just as a cesspool, when struck with a stick or a clod of earth, becomes even more foul-smelling, so too, a certain person here is prone to anger and full of distress;
even when spoken to slightly, he becomes resentful, agitated, ill-tempered, and stubborn, manifesting anger, hatred, and resentment.
Such a person should be regarded with equanimity; he should not be associated with, nor followed, nor served, nor honored.
Why is that? Because one might think:
"He may revile me, he may abuse me, he may even do me harm.
Therefore, such a person should be looked upon with equanimity; they should not be associated with, nor followed, nor honored, nor served.
And what kind of person is one who should be associated with, followed, and honored? Here,
a certain person is virtuous and of noble character—
such a person is one who should be associated with, followed, and honored.
For what reason?
Although one may not follow the example of such a person in terms of views, nevertheless, a good report concerning them spreads abroad:
"This person has a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous associate."
Therefore, such a person should be served, associated with, and attended upon.
And what kind of person is one who fulfills virtuous conduct but is only partial in concentration and partial in wisdom?
It is the stream-enterer and the once-returner.
These are called persons who are perfect in their virtues, moderate in concentration, and moderate in wisdom.
And what kind of person is one who is perfect in virtues, perfect in concentration, and moderate in wisdom?
It is the non-returner (anāgāmī).
This person is called one who fulfills both virtue and concentration, but practices wisdom only to a moderate degree.
And what kind of person fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom?
It is the Arahant.
This person is called one who fulfills morality, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom.
In this regard, who are the three kinds of teachers?
Here, a certain teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, but does not proclaim the full understanding of form, nor does he proclaim the full understanding of feelings.
Now, here a certain teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, proclaims the full understanding of forms, but does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings.
Here, another teacher proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, proclaims the full understanding of forms, and proclaims the full understanding of feelings.

In this regard, that teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, but does not proclaim the full understanding of forms, nor the full understanding of feelings, should be understood as a teacher who has attained the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*).

In this regard, that teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures and the full understanding of forms, but does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings—such a teacher should be understood as one who has attained the meditative absorptions of the formless realm.

In this regard, that teacher who proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings—such a teacher should be understood as a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).
These are the three types of teachers.
In this regard, who are the other three teachers?
Here, one teacher describes the self as real and substantial both in the present life and in future lives.
But here, another teacher describes the self as real and substantial in the present life, yet does not describe the self as real and substantial in future lives.
Now, here some teacher does not describe a self as real and established either in this present life or in the future life.
In that regard, the teacher who describes a self as real and established both in this present life and in the future life is to be regarded as an eternalist teacher.

In this regard, that teacher who describes the self as real and substantial in the present life, but does not describe the self as real and substantial in the future life—such a teacher is to be regarded as an annihilationist.

In this regard, that teacher who does not describe the self as real and substantial in the present life, nor does he describe the self as real and substantial in the future life—such a teacher is to be regarded as a Perfectly Enlightened One.
These are three other types of teachers.
The Exposition of the Triads.
